name: Number Series
blurb: A row of numbers follows a rule. What comes next?
childIntro: Look at the numbers going along the row. Work out what is happening, then say what comes next.
howItWorks: A string of numbers ending in a blank. It appears only at OLSAT levels D through G, so grade 3 upwards, because Quantitative Reasoning does not exist at the lower levels. Note that the blank is not always at the end.
parentTip: One habit solves nearly all of these: write the gap between every pair of numbers underneath. If the gaps are all the same, that is the rule. If the gaps themselves form a pattern, that is the rule. If neither, check whether the odd and even positions are two separate sequences woven together.

figure.alt: A row of numbers: ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty, question mark.

questions.explanation: Each number is five more than the one before. Thirty plus five is thirty-five.
questions.strategy: Find the gap between the first two, then check it stays the same.

questions.prompt: What number goes in the gap?

figure.alt: A row of numbers with the third one missing.

questions.explanation: The step is five each time. Fifteen plus five is twenty, and twenty plus five is twenty-five, which matches.
questions.strategy: The blank is not always at the end. Use the numbers on both sides of it.

figure.alt: A row where every other number is five.

questions.explanation: Two sequences are woven together. The numbers in the odd positions are all five. The ones in between go zero, one, two, so three comes next.
questions.strategy: When one number keeps repeating, ignore it and read only the others.

figure.alt: A row of numbers: two, five, nine, fourteen, twenty, question mark.

questions.explanation: The gaps are three, four, five, six. Each gap is one bigger than the last, so the next gap is seven. Twenty plus seven is twenty-seven.
questions.strategy: Write the gaps underneath. A pattern in the gaps is still a pattern.

figure.alt: A row of numbers that alternate between multiplying and dividing.

questions.explanation: The rule alternates: times three, then halve. Four times three is twelve. Twelve halved is six. Six times three is eighteen. Eighteen halved is nine. Nine times three is twenty-seven. Twenty-seven times three is eighty-one, because it is the multiplying step's turn again. Choice b halves instead.
questions.strategy: Two rules taking turns. Work out whose turn it is before you answer.

figure.alt: A row of numbers falling by nine each time.

questions.explanation: Each number is nine less than the one before. Forty-five minus nine is thirty-six. These are also the nine times table read backwards.
questions.strategy: Recognizing a times table saves time. Nine, eighteen, twenty-seven, thirty-six.

figure.alt: A row of numbers getting ten times smaller each step.

questions.explanation: Each number is a tenth of the one before, so the decimal point shifts one place left each time.
questions.strategy: Dividing by ten moves the decimal point one place to the left.

figure.alt: A row of square numbers.

questions.explanation: These are the square numbers: one times one, two times two, three times three and so on. The next is seven times seven, which is forty-nine. The gaps also tell you: three, five, seven, nine, eleven, then thirteen.
questions.strategy: Learn the first ten square numbers. They appear again and again.

figure.alt: A row of numbers that alternate between doubling and subtracting.

questions.explanation: The rule alternates: double, then take away one. Three doubled is six. Six minus one is five. Five doubled is ten. Ten minus one is nine. Nine doubled is eighteen. Eighteen minus one is seventeen.
questions.strategy: Two rules taking turns. Check both directions: up then down.

figure.alt: A row where each number is the sum of the two before it.

questions.explanation: Each number is made by adding the two before it. One and one is two. One and two is three. Two and three is five. Three and five is eight. Five and eight is thirteen.
questions.strategy: If the gaps do not help, try adding the two previous numbers together.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: Two more each time. Ten plus two is twelve. Choice b adds only one.
questions.strategy: Say the numbers out loud. Even numbers go two, four, six, eight, ten, twelve.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: Five less each time. Twenty-five minus five is twenty. Choice c skipped two steps at once.
questions.strategy: Check the size of one step, then take exactly one more step.

questions.prompt: What number goes in the gap?

figure.alt: A row of numbers with the middle one missing.

questions.explanation: The step is six. Twelve plus six is eighteen, and eighteen plus six is twenty-four, which matches the number after the gap.
questions.strategy: When the gap is in the middle, check your answer works on BOTH sides.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: Each number is three times the one before. Twenty-seven times three is eighty-one. Choice b is double, not triple.
questions.strategy: If the gaps grow fast, try multiplying rather than adding.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: Every number appears twice, and the pairs go up by seven: seven, fourteen, twenty-one. So the next pair starts at twenty-eight.
questions.strategy: When numbers repeat in pairs, read only the first of each pair.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: Two lists take turns. The first, third and fifth numbers are three, four, five. The second, fourth and sixth are eight, nine, ten. It is the first list's turn, so six comes next.
questions.strategy: Circle every other number and read them as their own list.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: The gaps are one, two, three, four, five. Each gap is one bigger, so the next gap is six. Sixteen plus six is twenty-two.
questions.strategy: Write the gaps underneath. A pattern in the gaps is still a pattern.

figure.alt: A row of numbers: 800, 400, 200, 100, question mark.

questions.explanation: Each number is half the one before. Half of one hundred is fifty. Choice b halves twice instead of once.
questions.strategy: Halving repeatedly gets small fast. Halve once per step, not twice.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: The rule alternates: times three, then minus three. Two times three is six. Six minus three is three. Three times three is nine. Nine minus three is six. Six times three is eighteen. Eighteen minus three is fifteen. Fifteen times three is forty-five.
questions.strategy: Up, down, up, down means two rules taking turns. Find both before you answer.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: The gaps are two, three, four, five, so the next gap is six. Fifteen plus six is twenty-one. These are the triangle numbers: one, then one plus two, then one plus two plus three, and so on.
questions.strategy: Growing gaps mean the total grows faster each step.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: This is the nine times table. Nine more each time, so forty-five plus nine is fifty-four.
questions.strategy: Recognizing a times table is faster than counting the gap.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: Twelve less each time. One hundred and eight minus twelve is ninety-six.
questions.strategy: Subtracting twelve is the same as taking ten and then two more.

questions.prompt: What number goes in the gap?

figure.alt: A row of numbers with the third one missing.

questions.explanation: Each number is five times the one before. Twenty-five times five is one hundred and twenty-five, and that times five is six hundred and twenty-five, which matches.
questions.strategy: Check a middle answer against the number on both sides of it.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: Each number is a number multiplied by itself three times: one times one times one, two times two times two, three times three times three, four times four times four. Next is five times five times five, which is one hundred and twenty-five. Choice c is nine times nine, a square not a cube.
questions.strategy: If the numbers grow very fast, check for cubes as well as squares.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: Each number is the two before it added together. Thirteen plus twenty-one is thirty-four.
questions.strategy: When the gaps do not repeat, try adding the two previous numbers.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: Each number doubles. One point six doubled is three point two. Choice b adds point eight instead of doubling.
questions.strategy: Doubling a decimal works the same as doubling a whole number.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: The rule alternates: halve, then add four. Eighty halved is forty. Forty plus four is forty-four. Forty-four halved is twenty-two. Twenty-two plus four is twenty-six. Twenty-six halved is thirteen. Thirteen plus four is seventeen. Choice b halves when it should add.
questions.strategy: Write the operation between each pair. The pattern is in the operations, not the numbers.

questions.prompt: What number goes in the gap?

figure.alt: A row of numbers with the fourth one missing.

questions.explanation: Each number is double the one before plus one. Three doubled plus one is seven. Seven doubled plus one is fifteen. Fifteen doubled plus one is thirty-one. And thirty-one doubled plus one is sixty-three, which matches the last number.
questions.strategy: Double-then-add-one is a common rule. Test it on the numbers you already have.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: Two lists take turns. The first, third, fifth and seventh numbers count one, two, three, four. The others go four, eight, twelve, which is the four times table. It is the second list's turn, so sixteen comes next.
questions.strategy: When two lists interleave, work out which one the blank belongs to first.

figure.alt: A row of numbers ending in a question mark.

questions.explanation: These are the prime numbers, which can only be divided by one and by themselves. After seventeen comes nineteen. Eighteen, twenty and twenty-one can all be split into equal groups, and twenty-three skips nineteen.
questions.strategy: When the gaps look random, check whether the numbers themselves are special.
